sin^{2}x + cos^{2}x = 1.title: Pythagorean identity
sin^{2}x + cos^{2}x = 1.about: On the unit circle the point at angle x is (cos x, sin x), and its distance from the origin is 1, so the squares add to 1. Use it to get cos x from sin x (or back), and to swap sin^{2} for 1 − cos^{2} when simplifying.
assumptions: Holds for every real (or complex) x
Solving for one function gives a ± sign; pick it from the quadrant of x
vars: angle (any real number, in radians or degrees)

example.problem: x is in the second quadrant with sin x = 3/5. Find cos x.
steps: cos x = ±4/5; cosine is negative in quadrant II

1 + tan^{2}x = sec^{2}x.title: Pythagorean identity for tan and sec
1 + tan^{2}x = sec^{2}x.about: Divide sin^{2}x + cos^{2}x = 1 by cos^{2}x. It links tangent and secant, and is the substitution behind ∫sec^{2}x dx and the x = a tan θ trick in integrals with a^{2} + x^{2}.
assumptions: cos x ≠ 0 (x ≠ π/2 + kπ), where tan and sec are undefined
vars: angle (any real number, in radians or degrees)

example.problem: tan x = 2 with x in quadrant I. Find sec x and cos x.

1 + cot^{2}x = csc^{2}x.title: Pythagorean identity for cot and csc
1 + cot^{2}x = csc^{2}x.about: Divide sin^{2}x + cos^{2}x = 1 by sin^{2}x. It links cotangent and cosecant, and turns 1 + cot^{2} into a single square.
assumptions: sin x ≠ 0 (x ≠ kπ), where cot and csc are undefined
vars: angle (any real number, in radians or degrees)

csc x = 1/sin x.title: Cosecant, the reciprocal of sine
csc x = 1/sin x.about: Cosecant is defined as one over sine. Calculators rarely have a csc key, so you evaluate it as 1/sin.
vars: angle (any real number, in radians or degrees)

sec x = 1/cos x.title: Secant, the reciprocal of cosine
sec x = 1/cos x.about: Secant is defined as one over cosine. It shows up in derivatives (d/dx tan x = sec^{2}x) and in the length of a slanted line.
assumptions: cos x ≠ 0, so x ≠ π/2 + kπ
vars: angle (any real number, in radians or degrees)

cot x = 1/tan x.title: Cotangent, the reciprocal of tangent
cot x = 1/tan x.about: Cotangent is one over tangent, or equivalently cos x/sin x. Use the quotient form where tan x is undefined (cot 90° = 0).
assumptions: tan x ≠ 0 and defined; at x = π/2 + kπ use cot x = cos x/sin x = 0 instead
vars: angle (any real number, in radians or degrees)
related: cot x = cos x / sin x
quotient form, defined wherever sin x ≠ 0
tan x = sin x / cos x

tan x = sin x / cos x.title: Tangent as a quotient
tan x = sin x / cos x.about: Tangent is the ratio of the unit-circle point's y to its x, which is the slope of the ray at angle x. Rewriting tan in sines and cosines is the usual first step in proving an identity.
vars: angle (any real number, in radians or degrees)
related: cot x = cos x / sin x

example.problem: sin x = 0.6 and cos x = 0.8. Find tan x.

cot x = cos x / sin x.title: Cotangent as a quotient
cot x = cos x / sin x.about: Cotangent is x over y for the unit-circle point, the reciprocal of tangent. This form stays defined at π/2, where tan is not.
vars: angle (any real number, in radians or degrees)
related: tan x = sin x / cos x

sin(π/2 − x) = cos x.title: Cofunction: sine of the complement
sin(π/2 − x) = cos x.about: In a right triangle the two acute angles add to 90°, and the side opposite one is adjacent to the other. So the sine of an angle is the cosine of its complement — the "co" in cosine.
assumptions: Holds for all x; π/2 is 90° when working in degrees
vars: angle (any real number, in radians or degrees)
related: sin(x − y) = sin x cos y − cos x sin y

example.problem: Write sin 70° as a cosine and check it.

cos(π/2 − x) = sin x.title: Cofunction: cosine of the complement
cos(π/2 − x) = sin x.about: The cosine of an angle equals the sine of its complement, from the right triangle with acute angles x and 90° − x.
vars: angle (any real number, in radians or degrees)
related: cos(x − y) = cos x cos y + sin x sin y

tan(π/2 − x) = cot x.title: Cofunction: tangent of the complement
tan(π/2 − x) = cot x.about: Swapping to the complementary angle swaps opposite and adjacent sides, so tangent becomes cotangent.
assumptions: x ≠ kπ, where cot x is undefined
vars: angle (any real number, in radians or degrees)

cot(π/2 − x) = tan x.title: Cofunction: cotangent of the complement
cot(π/2 − x) = tan x.about: Cotangent of the complementary angle is tangent, because the opposite and adjacent sides swap roles.
assumptions: x ≠ π/2 + kπ, where tan x is undefined
vars: angle (any real number, in radians or degrees)

sec(π/2 − x) = csc x.title: Cofunction: secant of the complement
sec(π/2 − x) = csc x.about: Secant is 1/cos and cosecant is 1/sin, so the cos ↔ sin cofunction identity carries over to their reciprocals.
vars: angle (any real number, in radians or degrees)

csc(π/2 − x) = sec x.title: Cofunction: cosecant of the complement
csc(π/2 − x) = sec x.about: Cosecant of the complement is secant: the reciprocal of sin(π/2 − x) = cos x.
vars: angle (any real number, in radians or degrees)

sin(−x) = −sin x.title: Sine is odd
sin(−x) = −sin x.about: Reflecting the angle across the x-axis flips the unit-circle point's y-coordinate, so sine changes sign. Sine's graph is symmetric about the origin.
vars: angle (any real number, in radians or degrees)

cos(−x) = cos x.title: Cosine is even
cos(−x) = cos x.about: Reflecting the angle across the x-axis leaves the unit-circle point's x-coordinate unchanged, so cosine does not change. Its graph is symmetric about the y-axis.
vars: angle (any real number, in radians or degrees)

tan(−x) = −tan x.title: Tangent is odd
tan(−x) = −tan x.about: Tangent is sin/cos: an odd function over an even one, so it is odd.
vars: angle (any real number, in radians or degrees)

sin(x + y) = sin x cos y + cos x sin y.title: Sine of a sum
sin(x + y) = sin x cos y + cos x sin y.about: Breaks the sine of a sum into the sines and cosines of the parts. It gives exact values at angles like 75° = 45° + 30°, and the double-angle formula follows with y = x.
assumptions: Holds for all x and y
vars: angle (any real number, in radians or degrees)
related: sin(x − y) = sin x cos y − cos x sin y
cos(x + y) = cos x cos y − sin x sin y

sin(x − y) = sin x cos y − cos x sin y.title: Sine of a difference
sin(x − y) = sin x cos y − cos x sin y.about: The sum formula with −y in place of y, using cos(−y) = cos y and sin(−y) = −sin y.
assumptions: Holds for all x and y
vars: angle (any real number, in radians or degrees)
related: sin(x + y) = sin x cos y + cos x sin y
cos(x − y) = cos x cos y + sin x sin y

cos(x + y) = cos x cos y − sin x sin y.title: Cosine of a sum
cos(x + y) = cos x cos y − sin x sin y.about: Breaks the cosine of a sum into products of the parts' sines and cosines; note the minus sign. With y = x it gives the double-angle forms of cos 2x.
assumptions: Holds for all x and y
vars: angle (any real number, in radians or degrees)
related: cos(x − y) = cos x cos y + sin x sin y

cos(x − y) = cos x cos y + sin x sin y.title: Cosine of a difference
cos(x − y) = cos x cos y + sin x sin y.about: The sum formula with −y for y. It is often the one proved first (from the distance between two unit-circle points), and the others follow from it.
assumptions: Holds for all x and y
vars: angle (any real number, in radians or degrees)
related: cos(x + y) = cos x cos y − sin x sin y
sin(x − y) = sin x cos y − cos x sin y

tan(x + y) = (tan x + tan y)/(1 − tan x.title: Tangent of a sum
tan(x + y) = (tan x + tan y)/(1 − tan x.about: Divide sin(x + y) by cos(x + y) and then divide top and bottom by cos x cos y. Handy when you know the tangents (slopes) of two angles and want the angle they add to.
assumptions: tan x, tan y and tan(x + y) defined: cos x, cos y ≠ 0 and tan x tan y ≠ 1
vars: angle (any real number, in radians or degrees)
related: tan(x − y) = (tan x − tan y)/(1 + tan x tan y)

tan(x − y) = (tan x − tan y)/(1 + tan x.title: Tangent of a difference
tan(x − y) = (tan x − tan y)/(1 + tan x.about: The sum formula with −y for y. With slopes m_{1} = tan x and m_{2} = tan y it gives the angle between two lines.
assumptions: tan x, tan y defined and tan x tan y ≠ −1 (perpendicular lines)
vars: angle (any real number, in radians or degrees)
related: tan(x + y) = (tan x + tan y)/(1 − tan x tan y)

example.problem: Find the acute angle between lines of slope 3 and 1.

sin 2x = 2 sin x cos x.title: Double angle for sine
sin 2x = 2 sin x cos x.about: The sine-of-a-sum formula with y = x. Use it to collapse sin x cos x into one sine, or to expand sin 2x when solving equations.
vars: angle (any real number, in radians or degrees)
related: sin(x + y) = sin x cos y + cos x sin y
sin x cos y = ½[sin(x + y) + sin(x − y)]

example.problem: sin x = 3/5 with x in quadrant I. Find sin 2x.

cos 2x = cos^{2}x − sin^{2}x.title: Double angle for cosine
cos 2x = cos^{2}x − sin^{2}x.about: The cosine-of-a-sum formula with y = x. Replacing sin^{2} or cos^{2} with the Pythagorean identity gives the two other forms.
vars: angle (any real number, in radians or degrees)

example.problem: sin x = 3/5, cos x = 4/5. Find cos 2x.

cos 2x = 2cos^{2}x − 1.title: Double angle for cosine, in cosine only
cos 2x = 2cos^{2}x − 1.about: Substitute sin^{2}x = 1 − cos^{2}x into cos^{2}x − sin^{2}x. Solved for cos^{2}x it becomes the power-reduction formula.
vars: angle (any real number, in radians or degrees)

cos 2x = 1 − 2sin^{2}x.title: Double angle for cosine, in sine only
cos 2x = 1 − 2sin^{2}x.about: Substitute cos^{2}x = 1 − sin^{2}x into cos^{2}x − sin^{2}x. Solved for sin^{2}x it becomes the power-reduction formula.
vars: angle (any real number, in radians or degrees)

tan 2x = 2 tan x/(1 − tan^{2}x).title: Double angle for tangent
tan 2x = 2 tan x/(1 − tan^{2}x).about: The tangent-of-a-sum formula with y = x. Gives tan 2x straight from tan x.
assumptions: tan x defined and tan^{2}x ≠ 1 (x ≠ π/4 + kπ/2, where tan 2x is undefined)
vars: angle (any real number, in radians or degrees)
related: tan(x + y) = (tan x + tan y)/(1 − tan x tan y)

sin(x/2) = ±√((1 − cos x)/2).title: Half angle for sine
sin(x/2) = ±√((1 − cos x)/2).about: Power reduction sin^{2}θ = (1 − cos 2θ)/2 with θ = x/2. Gives exact sines of angles like 15° and 22.5°.
assumptions: The sign is the sign of sin(x/2), set by the quadrant of x/2, not of x
vars: angle (any real number, in radians or degrees)

cos(x/2) = ±√((1 + cos x)/2).title: Half angle for cosine
cos(x/2) = ±√((1 + cos x)/2).about: Power reduction cos^{2}θ = (1 + cos 2θ)/2 with θ = x/2.
assumptions: The sign is the sign of cos(x/2), set by the quadrant of x/2
vars: angle (any real number, in radians or degrees)

tan(x/2) = (1 − cos x)/sin x.title: Half angle for tangent (no ± sign)
tan(x/2) = (1 − cos x)/sin x.about: Divide the sine and cosine half-angle forms and rationalize. Unlike those, this form carries its own sign, so no quadrant check is needed.
vars: angle (any real number, in radians or degrees)

tan(x/2) = sin x/(1 + cos x).title: Half angle for tangent, second form
tan(x/2) = sin x/(1 + cos x).about: Multiply (1 − cos x)/sin x by (1 + cos x)/(1 + cos x) and use 1 − cos^{2}x = sin^{2}x. Also the basis of the Weierstrass substitution t = tan(x/2) in integrals.
vars: angle (any real number, in radians or degrees)

sin^{2}x = (1 − cos 2x)/2.title: Power reduction for sin²
sin^{2}x = (1 − cos 2x)/2.about: Trades a square for a first power of cosine at double the angle. The standard way to integrate sin^{2}x and to find the average of a squared sinusoid (it is ½).
vars: angle (any real number, in radians or degrees)

cos^{2}x = (1 + cos 2x)/2.title: Power reduction for cos²
cos^{2}x = (1 + cos 2x)/2.about: Trades a square of cosine for a first power at double the angle. Used to integrate cos^{2}x and to find RMS values.
vars: angle (any real number, in radians or degrees)

example.problem: Find cos^{2}(15°) without a calculator's cos 15°.

tan^{2}x = (1 − cos 2x)/(1 + cos 2x).title: Power reduction for tan²
tan^{2}x = (1 − cos 2x)/(1 + cos 2x).about: The sin^{2} power-reduction formula divided by the cos^{2} one.
vars: angle (any real number, in radians or degrees)

sin x sin y = ½[cos(x − y) − cos(x + y)].title: Product to sum: sin·sin
sin x sin y = ½[cos(x − y) − cos(x + y)].about: Subtract cos(x + y) from cos(x − y) and halve. Turns a product into a sum, which is easier to integrate and shows the beat frequencies when two waves multiply.
assumptions: Holds for all x and y
vars: angle (any real number, in radians or degrees)
related: cos x cos y = ½[cos(x − y) + cos(x + y)]
cos x − cos y = −2 sin((x + y)/2) sin((x − y)/2)

example.problem: Write sin 75° sin 15° as a sum and evaluate.

cos x cos y = ½[cos(x − y) + cos(x + y)].title: Product to sum: cos·cos
cos x cos y = ½[cos(x − y) + cos(x + y)].about: Add the cosine sum and difference formulas and halve. Used in integrating products of cosines and in mixing signals (two frequencies multiply into their sum and difference).
assumptions: Holds for all x and y
vars: angle (any real number, in radians or degrees)
related: sin x sin y = ½[cos(x − y) − cos(x + y)]
cos x + cos y = 2 cos((x + y)/2) cos((x − y)/2)

example.problem: Write cos 75° cos 15° as a sum and evaluate.

sin x cos y = ½[sin(x + y) + sin(x − y)].title: Product to sum: sin·cos
sin x cos y = ½[sin(x + y) + sin(x − y)].about: Add the sine sum and difference formulas and halve.
assumptions: Holds for all x and y
vars: angle (any real number, in radians or degrees)
related: cos x sin y = ½[sin(x + y) − sin(x − y)]
sin x + sin y = 2 sin((x + y)/2) cos((x − y)/2)

example.problem: Write sin 75° cos 15° as a sum and evaluate.

cos x sin y = ½[sin(x + y) − sin(x − y)].title: Product to sum: cos·sin
cos x sin y = ½[sin(x + y) − sin(x − y)].about: Subtract the sine difference formula from the sum formula and halve.
assumptions: Holds for all x and y
vars: angle (any real number, in radians or degrees)
related: sin x cos y = ½[sin(x + y) + sin(x − y)]
sin x − sin y = 2 cos((x + y)/2) sin((x − y)/2)

example.problem: Write cos 75° sin 15° as a sum and evaluate.

sin x + sin y = 2 sin((x + y)/2) cos((x.title: Sum to product: sin + sin
sin x + sin y = 2 sin((x + y)/2) cos((x.about: Turns a sum of sines into a product, which is what you need to solve sin x + sin y = 0 or to see beats when two close frequencies add.
assumptions: Holds for all x and y
vars: angle (any real number, in radians or degrees)
related: sin x − sin y = 2 cos((x + y)/2) sin((x − y)/2)
sin x cos y = ½[sin(x + y) + sin(x − y)]

sin x − sin y = 2 cos((x + y)/2) sin((x.title: Sum to product: sin − sin
sin x − sin y = 2 cos((x + y)/2) sin((x.about: Turns a difference of sines into a product.
assumptions: Holds for all x and y
vars: angle (any real number, in radians or degrees)
related: sin x + sin y = 2 sin((x + y)/2) cos((x − y)/2)

cos x + cos y = 2 cos((x + y)/2) cos((x.title: Sum to product: cos + cos
cos x + cos y = 2 cos((x + y)/2) cos((x.about: Turns a sum of cosines into a product of cosines.
assumptions: Holds for all x and y
vars: angle (any real number, in radians or degrees)
related: cos x − cos y = −2 sin((x + y)/2) sin((x − y)/2)
cos x cos y = ½[cos(x − y) + cos(x + y)]

cos x − cos y = −2 sin((x + y)/2) sin((x.title: Sum to product: cos − cos
cos x − cos y = −2 sin((x + y)/2) sin((x.about: Turns a difference of cosines into a product of sines; mind the leading minus sign.
assumptions: Holds for all x and y
vars: angle (any real number, in radians or degrees)
related: cos x + cos y = 2 cos((x + y)/2) cos((x − y)/2)
sin x sin y = ½[cos(x − y) − cos(x + y)]

log_{b}(xy) = log_{b}x + log_{b}y.title: Log of a product
log_{b}(xy) = log_{b}x + log_{b}y.about: A logarithm turns multiplication into addition, because b^{m}b^{n} = b^{m+n}. This is why decibels and pH add when the underlying ratios multiply.
assumptions: x > 0 and y > 0 (logs of zero or negatives are not real)
vars: base of the logarithm, b > 0 and b ≠ 1
positive number whose log is taken

log_{b}(x/y) = log_{b}x − log_{b}y.title: Log of a quotient
log_{b}(x/y) = log_{b}x − log_{b}y.about: A logarithm turns division into subtraction. A ratio's log is the difference of the logs, as in a gain in dB.
assumptions: x > 0 and y > 0 (logs of zero or negatives are not real)
vars: base of the logarithm, b > 0 and b ≠ 1
positive number whose log is taken

example.problem: Given ln 10 ≈ 2.3026 and ln 2 ≈ 0.6931, find ln 5.

log_{b}(x^{r}) = r log_{b}x.title: Log of a power
log_{b}(x^{r}) = r log_{b}x.about: A logarithm brings an exponent down as a multiplier. This is how you solve for an unknown exponent: take logs of both sides.
vars: base of the logarithm, b > 0 and b ≠ 1
positive number whose log is taken

steps: ln(2^{x}) = ln 50, so x ln 2 = ln 50

log_{b}x = ln x / ln b.title: Change of base
log_{b}x = ln x / ln b.about: Any logarithm can be written with natural logs (or common logs) as a ratio. This is how a calculator with only ln and log finds log_{2} or log_{7}.
assumptions: Any other base works in place of e: log_{b}x = log_{c}x / log_{c}b
vars: base of the logarithm, b > 0 and b ≠ 1
positive number whose log is taken
related: power rule, used to prove it

log_{b}1 = 0.title: Log of 1 is zero
log_{b}1 = 0.about: Any allowed base raised to the power 0 is 1, so the log of 1 is 0 in every base.
vars: base of the logarithm, b > 0 and b ≠ 1

log_{b}b = 1.title: Log of the base is one
log_{b}b = 1.about: b^{1} = b, so the log of the base in its own base is 1. With the power rule it gives log_{b}(b^{x}) = x.
vars: base of the logarithm, b > 0 and b ≠ 1

log_{b}(b^{x}) = x.title: Log undoes the exponential
log_{b}(b^{x}) = x.about: log_{b} and b^{x} are inverse functions: raising b to a power and then taking log_{b} returns the power.
vars: base of the logarithm, b > 0 and b ≠ 1

b^{log_{b}x} = x.title: Exponential undoes the log
b^{log_{b}x} = x.about: Raising b to the log_{b} of x returns x. Use it to rewrite any power with a convenient base: a^{x} = e^{x ln a}.
vars: base of the logarithm, b > 0 and b ≠ 1
positive number whose log is taken

ln(e^{x}) = x.title: Natural log undoes e^{x}
ln(e^{x}) = x.about: ln is the logarithm with base e ≈ 2.71828, so it undoes the natural exponential. Used to pull a variable out of an exponent, as in solving for time in exponential decay.

example.problem: A quantity decays as N = N_{0}e^{−0.2t}. When is N = N_{0}/2?

e^{ln x} = x.title: e^{x} undoes the natural log
e^{ln x} = x.about: Exponentiating a natural log returns the number. Used to undo ln after solving, and to write powers as a^{x} = e^{x ln a}.

a^{m}a^{n} = a^{m+n}.title: Product of powers
a^{m}a^{n} = a^{m+n}.about: Multiplying powers of the same base adds their exponents: m factors of a times n factors of a is m + n factors.
assumptions: Integer exponents: any a (a ≠ 0 if an exponent is negative)

a^{m}/a^{n} = a^{m−n}.title: Quotient of powers
a^{m}/a^{n} = a^{m−n}.about: Dividing powers of the same base subtracts exponents: the n factors in the bottom cancel n of the m on top.

(a^{m})^{n} = a^{mn}.title: Power of a power
(a^{m})^{n} = a^{mn}.about: Raising a power to a power multiplies the exponents: n copies of m factors.

(ab)^{n} = a^{n}b^{n}.title: Power of a product
(ab)^{n} = a^{n}b^{n}.about: An exponent distributes over multiplication (but not over addition: (a + b)^{2} ≠ a^{2} + b^{2}).

a^{0} = 1.title: Zero exponent
a^{0} = 1.about: Any nonzero number to the power 0 is 1, which keeps a^{m}/a^{m} = a^{m−m} consistent.
assumptions: a ≠ 0 (0^{0} is undefined, though often taken as 1 in series and combinatorics)

a^{−n} = 1/a^{n}.title: Negative exponent
a^{−n} = 1/a^{n}.about: A negative exponent means the reciprocal. Moving a factor across the fraction bar flips the sign of its exponent.

a^{1/n} = ^{n}√a.title: Fractional exponent as a root
a^{1/n} = ^{n}√a.about: The power 1/n is the nth root, because (a^{1/n})^{n} = a^{1} = a. Then a^{m/n} = (^{n}√a)^{m}.
assumptions: a ≥ 0 for even n; any real a for odd n

(a + b)^{2} = a^{2} + 2ab + b^{2}.title: Square of a sum
(a + b)^{2} = a^{2} + 2ab + b^{2}.about: Expanding (a + b)(a + b) gives the cross term 2ab, which is what's missed when people write a^{2} + b^{2}. Read backward it is the pattern for completing the square.
assumptions: Holds for all real (or complex) a and b

(a − b)^{2} = a^{2} − 2ab + b^{2}.title: Square of a difference
(a − b)^{2} = a^{2} − 2ab + b^{2}.about: The square of a sum with −b for b: the cross term turns negative.
assumptions: Holds for all real (or complex) a and b

a^{2} − b^{2} = (a + b)(a − b).title: Difference of squares
a^{2} − b^{2} = (a + b)(a − b).about: Factors a difference of two squares; the cross terms cancel. Used to factor, to rationalize (multiply by the conjugate) and for quick products like 31 · 29.
assumptions: Holds for all real (or complex) a and b
A sum of squares a^{2} + b^{2} does not factor over the reals

a^{3} + b^{3} = (a + b)(a^{2} − ab + b^{.title: Sum of cubes
a^{3} + b^{3} = (a + b)(a^{2} − ab + b^{.about: Factors a sum of two cubes. The quadratic factor has no real roots, so a + b is the only real linear factor.
assumptions: Holds for all real (or complex) a and b

example.problem: Factor x^{3} + 8 and check at x = 2.

a^{3} − b^{3} = (a − b)(a^{2} + ab + b^{.title: Difference of cubes
a^{3} − b^{3} = (a − b)(a^{2} + ab + b^{.about: Factors a difference of two cubes. a − b is the only real linear factor.
assumptions: Holds for all real (or complex) a and b

example.problem: Factor x^{3} − 27 and check at x = 5.

(a + b)^{3} = a^{3} + 3a^{2}b + 3ab^{2}.title: Cube of a sum
(a + b)^{3} = a^{3} + 3a^{2}b + 3ab^{2}.about: The binomial theorem for n = 3; the coefficients 1, 3, 3, 1 are row 3 of Pascal's triangle.
assumptions: Holds for all real (or complex) a and b

(a − b)^{3} = a^{3} − 3a^{2}b + 3ab^{2}.title: Cube of a difference
(a − b)^{3} = a^{3} − 3a^{2}b + 3ab^{2}.about: The cube of a sum with −b for b: the signs alternate.
assumptions: Holds for all real (or complex) a and b

(a + b)^{n} = Σ_{k=0}^{n} C(n, k) a^{n−k.title: Binomial theorem
(a + b)^{n} = Σ_{k=0}^{n} C(n, k) a^{n−k.about: Expands any whole-number power of a sum. The coefficient of a^{n−k}b^{k} is C(n, k) = n!/(k!(n − k)!), the number of ways to choose which k of the n factors give a b.
assumptions: n a non-negative integer (for other n it becomes an infinite series, valid for |b/a| < 1)

example.problem: Find the coefficient of x^{3} in (2 + x)^{5}.

(px + q)/((x − a)(x − b)) = A/(x − a) +.title: Partial fractions: two distinct linear factors

Σ_{k=1}^{n} 1 = n.title: Sum of n ones
Σ_{k=1}^{n} 1 = n.about: Adding 1 once for each k from 1 to n gives n. More generally a constant c summed n times is cn.
vars: number of terms, a positive integer

Σ_{k=1}^{n} k = n(n + 1)/2.title: Sum of the first n integers
Σ_{k=1}^{n} k = n(n + 1)/2.about: Gauss's trick: pair 1 with n, 2 with n − 1, and so on; each pair sums to n + 1 and there are n/2 pairs. The triangular numbers.
vars: number of terms, a positive integer

Σ_{k=1}^{n} k^{2} = n(n + 1)(2n + 1)/6.title: Sum of the first n squares
Σ_{k=1}^{n} k^{2} = n(n + 1)(2n + 1)/6.about: Closed form for 1 + 4 + 9 + … + n^{2}. It appears in Riemann sums for ∫x^{2} dx and in moments of inertia of discrete masses.
vars: number of terms, a positive integer

Σ_{k=1}^{n} k^{3} = (n(n + 1)/2)^{2}.title: Sum of the first n cubes
Σ_{k=1}^{n} k^{3} = (n(n + 1)/2)^{2}.about: The sum of the first n cubes is the square of the sum of the first n integers (Nicomachus's theorem).
vars: number of terms, a positive integer

Σ_{k=1}^{n} (2k − 1) = n^{2}.title: Sum of the first n odd numbers
Σ_{k=1}^{n} (2k − 1) = n^{2}.about: 1 + 3 + 5 + … + (2n − 1) = n^{2}: each odd number adds an L-shaped border to an (n − 1) × (n − 1) square.
vars: number of terms, a positive integer

Σ_{k=1}^{n} (a + (k − 1)d) = n(2a + (n −.title: Arithmetic series
Σ_{k=1}^{n} (a + (k − 1)d) = n(2a + (n −.about: Sum of n terms that go up by a fixed step d. It equals n times the average of the first and last terms, n(a + ℓ)/2.
vars: number of terms, a positive integer

Σ_{k=1}^{n} ar^{k−1} = a(1 − r^{n})/(1 −.title: Finite geometric series
Σ_{k=1}^{n} ar^{k−1} = a(1 − r^{n})/(1 −.about: Sum of n terms each r times the last. Multiply the sum by r and subtract: everything but the first and last term cancels. Used for loan payments, compound growth and settling of feedback loops.
assumptions: r ≠ 1 (when r = 1 the sum is na)
vars: number of terms, a positive integer

Σ_{k=0}^{∞} ar^{k} = a/(1 − r).title: Infinite geometric series
Σ_{k=0}^{∞} ar^{k} = a/(1 − r).about: Let n → ∞ in the finite sum: r^{n} → 0 when |r| < 1. Gives repeating decimals as fractions, total distance of a bouncing ball, and the 1/(1 − z^{−1}) of the z-transform.

Σ_{k=1}^{∞} kr^{k} = r/(1 − r)^{2}.title: Arithmetic–geometric series
Σ_{k=1}^{∞} kr^{k} = r/(1 − r)^{2}.about: Differentiate Σ r^{k} = 1/(1 − r) with respect to r and multiply by r. It gives expected values such as the mean of a geometric distribution.
related: the series it is derived from

Σ_{k=0}^{∞} x^{k}/k! = e^{x}.title: Taylor series of e^{x}
Σ_{k=0}^{∞} x^{k}/k! = e^{x}.about: The exponential function's Maclaurin series. It converges for every x, and fast: a handful of terms gives e^{x} accurately for small x.
assumptions: Converges for every real or complex x

Σ_{k=0}^{n} C(n, k) = 2^{n}.title: Sum of binomial coefficients
Σ_{k=0}^{n} C(n, k) = 2^{n}.about: Set a = b = 1 in the binomial theorem. Counting: each of n items is either in or out of a subset, so there are 2^{n} subsets in all, and C(n, k) of them have size k.
vars: number of items, a non-negative integer
